**ETH Zurich — the attack that was a template, not a payload (2024)**

In June 2024 the SPY Lab at ETH Zurich — Edoardo Debenedetti, Jie Zhang, Mislav Balunović, Luca Beurer-Kellner, Marc Fischer and Florian Tramèr — published AgentDojo (arXiv 2406.13352; NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks). It is the closest thing the field has to a taxonomy with numbers attached. The benchmark holds 97 realistic user tasks across four stateful environments — a workspace of email, calendar and cloud storage, a banking client, a travel booking agent and a Slack workspace — and pairs them with injection tasks to give 629 security test cases. Critically, the attacker never speaks to the agent. The payload sits in an email body, a calendar invite, a product page or a channel message: content the agent pulls in through a tool call while doing something an innocent user asked for.

The taxonomic finding is that the strongest attack is a wrapper, not a string. AgentDojo's "Important message" attack frames the attacker's goal as an urgent instruction from a fabricated authority, addressed to the model and interpolating the real user's name, then appends whatever the injection task wants done — send this transfer, forward that file. The same wrapper carries any goal across all four environments. Against GPT-4o with no defence, the paper reports a 57.69% targeted attack success rate.

The second finding matters more for architecture: capability and robustness are separate axes. Claude 3.5 Sonnet led benign utility at 78.22% against GPT-4o's 69.00%, yet models that completed more tasks were not thereby harder to hijack, and even without any attack state-of-the-art models failed a large share of the tasks outright.

AgentDojo's real contribution is that it scores the user task and the injection task independently. A defence that refuses everything drives attack success to zero and utility to zero with it. The prompt-injection detector the authors evaluate cuts targeted success to 7.95% while dropping benign utility from 69.00% to 41.49% and utility under attack to 21.14% — a defence that would look excellent in any report quoting only the security number.

When you write the threat model for your own agent, enumerate channels rather than payloads: every tool whose output re-enters the context is a category, and each one needs its own test suite and its own pair of numbers. A taxonomy organised around clever strings ages out in a month. One organised around where untrusted text enters your loop is the thing you will still be measuring against next year.

**Lakera — a million players priced the filters (2023–2025)**

Most sanitization advice is written by the people who build sanitizers. Lakera did something harder: it turned its defences into a game and let the internet grade them. Gandalf, online since May 2023, asks players to talk a guarded model into revealing a password, with each level adding another layer — hardened system prompt, input blocklists, output checks, a separate guard model. The paper the team published in January 2025, "Gandalf the Red: Adaptive Security for LLMs" (arXiv 2501.07927), reports that more than one million players have submitted over 40 million prompts and password guesses, and releases Gandalf-RCT: 279,675 prompts across 36,239 sessions from 15,402 users, collected between 1 October and 7 November 2024.

The paper's framing, D-SEC, refuses to score security on its own. It separates attackers from legitimate users, models multi-step interaction rather than single prompts, and expresses security and utility together as something you can optimise. That is a deliberate rebuke to the usual benchmark, where a filter that blocks nine in ten benign requests scores beautifully.

The layered result is the one worth carrying into your own stack. At level D, where several defences are combined so that any one firing blocks the request, the share of players who beat the level was 2.9% in the general setup, 6.3% in summarisation and 6.4% in the topic-restricted setup. But the mechanism behind that number is the finding: only 14.5% of attacks were blocked by every defence. The layers were not redundant copies of one another catching the same crude attempts — they caught largely different attacks, which is the empirical case for defence-in-depth rather than for shopping for the single best classifier.

The cost side is measured too. Defences built into the model's own instructions degrade output quality even when they block nothing at all — the authors observe shorter responses and shifted content on benign traffic. The other lever that worked was scope: the restricted summarisation and topic setups were more defensible than the general one, because narrowing what the application is allowed to do narrows what an injection can ask for.

Your input validator is one of these layers, and it should be justified the same way — by what it catches that the others miss, not by its detection rate in isolation. Before you add another regex tier, measure the benign traffic it costs you, and check whether tightening the agent's permitted scope would have bought more security for less.

**Slack — the API key that left inside a link the assistant wrote (2024)**

On 20 August 2024 the security firm PromptArmor published a disclosure against Slack AI, and it is the cleanest published demonstration of output-channel exfiltration in a product people actually use. The setup needs no privilege: an attacker with an ordinary workspace account creates a public channel, joins it alone, and posts an instruction. Slack AI's retrieval treats public-channel content as searchable by every member of the workspace whether or not they have joined the channel, so that message is now eligible context for someone else's query.

The victim then asks Slack AI a legitimate question about their own data — say, for an API key sitting in a private channel the attacker cannot read. Retrieval assembles both: the private message the user is entitled to see, and the attacker's public instruction. PromptArmor's payload told the model to output "Error loading message, [click here to reauthenticate]", with the secret substituted into the link target. Slack renders the markdown, the user sees a plausible re-auth prompt, and the click sends the key to the attacker's server in the query string.

Nothing in the permission model was bypassed. The secret was read under the victim's own authority, and the exfiltration channel was the client's rendering of the assistant's own output — the model's text becomes the request. That is the property to internalise: once an interface renders links or images from generated content, your data-loss boundary is the URL allowlist, not the access-control list.

The blast radius then widened on its own. On 14 August 2024, days before the disclosure, Slack had extended Slack AI to draw in files from channels and DMs, which meant the instruction could ride in an uploaded document rather than a posted message — no human need ever read it. Slack's first response addressed the wrong layer: "Messages posted to public channels can be searched for and viewed by all Members of the Workspace, regardless if they are joined to the channel or not. This is intended behavior." After the write-up went public, Salesforce stated: "We've deployed a patch to address the issue and have no evidence at this time of unauthorized access to customer data."

The defensive decision this lesson is preparing you for sits at the render boundary, not the retrieval one. Decide which hosts your client may fetch from or link to, strip everything else, and treat a generated URL whose path or query carries context-derived text as a leak until proven otherwise. And when someone widens what your agent can read, re-run that boundary — the ingestion change was the real escalation here, not the payload.

**SAP — the escape that rode out through the service mesh (2024)**

SAP AI Core is a managed platform on which customers run their own training code, so executing untrusted code is not a risk the product accepts — it is the product. Containment therefore carries the entire security model. In research published on 17 July 2024 as "SAPwned", Wiz described five issues found by taking the ordinary customer path, submitting a training job, and asking what that pod could reach. The findings were reported to SAP on 25 January 2024; SAP fixed the first on 16 February and completed the remaining fixes by 15 May.

The escape did not touch the kernel. Customer pods ran behind an admission controller that blocked root and other dangerous options, with network policy enforced by an Istio sidecar. Two configuration choices defeated that. Setting shareProcessNamespace gave the workload visibility into the sidecar's process namespace, from which the researchers lifted an access token for Istiod. Setting the container's runAsUser to 1337 — the UID Istio's own proxy runs as, and therefore the UID excluded from Istio's iptables redirection so the mesh does not capture its own traffic — took the container's egress outside the mesh altogether. The enforcement point sat inside the blast radius it was meant to define.

What that unrestricted network reached was a lesson in internal services that assume the perimeter has already authenticated the caller. A Loki instance returned AWS S3 credentials from its /config endpoint. Six unauthenticated NFS shares on port 2049 held other customers' training code and datasets, organised by customer ID. A deprecated Helm Tiller server on port 44134 answered unauthenticated gRPC and yielded read/write credentials for SAP's Docker registry and Artifactory; deploying a package through it granted cluster-admin, exposing customer secrets for AWS, SAP HANA, Docker Hub and Google Container Registry — and with registry write access, the platform's own image supply chain. SAP remediated the issues and stated that no customer data was compromised.

The architectural reading is that isolation built as one strong boundary degrades to no boundary the moment the workload can speak as the thing enforcing it. Sidecar-based policy shares a failure domain with the pod it polices, and "the network is internal" is not authentication.

When you place an agent's code interpreter behind a container, the useful questions are not about the image. Ask whether the workload can impersonate or observe the component that enforces your egress policy; ask what an escaped process reaches on the network before it reaches anything you own; and assume the sandbox is already lost when you decide whether the services behind it require credentials of their own.

**Wells Fargo — the conversations that were never on the record (2023)**

On 8 August 2023 the US Securities and Exchange Commission announced charges against 11 firms for what it called widespread and longstanding failures to maintain and preserve electronic communications, with combined penalties of $289 million. Wells Fargo entities paid the largest single share, $125 million, and settled a parallel action with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission for a further $75 million. No fraud, mis-selling or client loss was alleged anywhere in it. The finding was that from at least 2019 staff discussed firm business on personal devices using WhatsApp, iMessage and Signal, and the firm could not produce those records.

The mechanism is that the obligation attaches to the channel, not to the content or the intent. Regulators did not weigh whether the missing messages were incriminating. The SEC's announcement records that the firms "admitted the facts set forth in their respective SEC orders, acknowledged that their conduct violated recordkeeping provisions of the federal securities laws" and had begun improving their compliance procedures. Bloomberg's account of the Wells Fargo order describes the head of an investment banking unit sending and receiving more than 1,000 business-related messages on unapproved channels — this was not shadow behaviour at the edges; it ran through the supervisory layer meant to enforce the policy.

Nor was it one firm's lapse. Banking Dive reported that by that point the SEC had brought 30 such actions yielding over $1.5 billion in penalties since 2021. When a control fails identically at that many institutions it was never a control, but a written instruction competing with a more convenient channel.

For audit design the distinction this draws is between tamper-evidence and coverage. An append-only, hash-chained log proves that what it captured has not been altered afterwards; it says nothing whatever about what never entered it. Coverage is the property an auditor actually tests, and it is decided long before the incident, by which paths of action were wired through the recording layer and which were left to convention.

Your agent has off-channel equivalents, and they are concrete: a direct SDK call that bypasses the logging proxy, a retry a framework swallows without emitting an event, an MCP server a developer side-loads onto their own machine, a batch run under a shared service account, a human override applied in a console. Enumerate every path by which the system can act, and decide for each whether it is on the record — before someone asks you to reconstruct what the agent did on a date eight months ago. Where a path cannot be captured, close the path; a policy forbidding it is what these firms already had.
